clue.text: Duty of extra esteem getting volunteers cross

parts.note: to esteem something is to value it
something extra is added on
the TA, the Territorial Army, is Britain's volunteer reserve force
a cross is the shape of the letter X

explanation.surface: A tax levied on extra regard makes volunteers angry.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads 'extra esteem' but the answer puts the esteem first; 'of' and 'getting' only link. The Territorial Army is Britain's volunteer reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: VAT is a duty in the sense of a tax charged on goods and services.

clue.text: A mere door, perhaps, to higher things?

definitions.text: A mere door, perhaps, to higher things?

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters might be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: Is a humble door perhaps a gateway to loftier matters?
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges A MERE DOOR; read whole, the clue describes an airfield as the door through which people go up into the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: An airfield is the place where flights take off, a doorway to the skies.

clue.text: Singular name for Diana's sister

definitions.meaning: oneness, the state of being single rather than many
Diana Mitford's sister was ... Mitford, one of the famous Mitford sisters

explanation.walkthrough: The Mitford sisters were a famous set of six aristocratic English sisters of the 1930s; Diana and Unity were two of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Oneness is the meaning of the word, matching the sense of being singular, and it was also a Mitford sister's first name.

clue.text: Free puff for a party?

parts.note: a puff is a promotional plug, an advertisement or ad
Lib is short for the Liberal party

explanation.surface: A free advertisement promoting a political party.
explanation.definitionFit: Improvised remarks are free in the sense of unscripted, said off the cuff.

clue.text: Gordon almost dead, confused and coerced

indicators.note: confused means the gathered letters are jumbled up
almost means the last letter of dead is dropped

explanation.surface: Gordon, nearly dead and muddled, was forced into it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims dead to DEA; 'confused' then rearranges GORDON plus DEA.
explanation.definitionFit: To be dragooned is to be forced or pressured into doing something, a synonym for coerced.

clue.text: Girl loses head, another gets up to start Bacchus's wild song of praise

indicators.note: losing its head means the girl's name drops its first letter

parts.note: Edith is a girl's name

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up means the name is read from bottom to top

parts.note: another girl, here Mary

indicators.note: to start means just the opening letter of Bacchus is used

explanation.surface: Two girls jostle to begin a hymn to the god of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses head' cuts EDITH to DITH; 'gets up' turns MARY to YRAM in this down entry; 'to start' takes B from Bacchus.
explanation.definitionFit: A dithyramb was an ecstatic choral hymn sung to Dionysus, so a wild song of praise.

clue.text: Love morning with the Guardian's appearance

parts.note: the clue appeared in the Guardian, so the paper's own is ours

explanation.surface: Affection makes a morning appearance in the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter writes for the Guardian, so 'the Guardian's' is OUR, as a paper speaking of itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Amour is a borrowed French word for love, especially a love affair.

clue.text: Without one, little children repeatedly tear loose, out of control

definitions.text: Without one, little children repeatedly tear loose, out of control

indicators.note: out of control means the letters run wild into a new order
repeatedly means the short form is used twice

parts.note: ch is an abbreviation for child or children

explanation.surface: Without a supervisor, small kids keep breaking free and running riot.
explanation.walkthrough: CH twice, from 'little children repeatedly', joins TEAR and LOOSE; 'out of control' rearranges them. Read whole, the clue says what happens in a class with nobody in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A classroom without its instructor is exactly where youngsters run wild.

clue.text: Where Hamlet slept with no alternative in Somerset?

definitions.text: Where Hamlet slept with no alternative in Somerset?

indicators.note: alternative signals a different arrangement of the letters

explanation.surface: Asks where Shakespeare's prince might have slept, if not in a castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alternative' rearranges HAMLET, SLEPT and NO; 'with' only joins. The question mark admits the place is a pun on a Somerset town, Somerset being a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: This market town lies in Somerset, and its name could be read as a spot where a hamlet slept.

clue.text: Warm, cold or laid back?

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

indicators.note: back means the word laid is turned round

explanation.surface: Asks whether something is hot, cold or simply relaxed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns LAID into DIAL; 'laid back' looks like the phrase meaning relaxed.
explanation.definitionFit: A cordial welcome is a warm, friendly one.

clue.text: City, a New Testament one with old church

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A biblical city with an ancient church.
explanation.definitionFit: Antioch was a major ancient city, an early centre of Christianity.

clue.text: Strangely divine, holy but not at first outwardly

indicators.note: outwardly means the shortened word sits around the other piece
not at first means holy loses its opening letter

parts.note: a divine is a cleric; DD, Doctor of Divinity, is a divine's degree

explanation.surface: A holy man who is strangely unlike his first impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not at first' cuts holy to OLY; 'outwardly' puts it around DD; 'but' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Oddly and strangely are synonyms, both meaning in an unusual way.

clue.text: One may catch, say, Labour's blunder on reflection

parts.note: a boob is a blunder

indicators.note: on reflection means the word is seen as in a mirror, backwards

parts.note: Labour is an example of a political party

explanation.surface: Thinking it over, Labour's mistake will trip someone up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on reflection' reads the party backwards; 'say' marks Labour as one example of a party, and 'One may catch' looks like a cricket fielder.
explanation.definitionFit: A booby trap is a hidden device set to catch the unwary.

clue.text: Battle leads English to freedom

parts.note: Loos was a First World War battle in 1915

explanation.surface: A battle brings English people their liberty.
explanation.walkthrough: The Battle of Loos was a British offensive in France in 1915. 'leads' and 'to' only join.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the loose means being at liberty, so the noun here means freedom.

clue.text: Inveterate, if erroneous, need to store corn

indicators.note: to store means the scrambled word holds the other piece inside
erroneous means the word need is wrongly arranged

parts.note: corn is grain

explanation.surface: A persistent mistake: needing somewhere to keep the harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'erroneous' scrambles need to ENED, and 'to store' wraps it around the corn; 'if' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Deeply ingrained habits are firmly fixed, which is what inveterate means.

clue.text: Republic, as in Roman style

indicators.note: in a Roman style hints at a reworking of the letters

explanation.surface: A state run in the manner of ancient Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'style' rearranges AS IN ROMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: This tiny state enclosed by Italy is one of the oldest republics in the world.

clue.text: Organise messy site clearance

indicators.note: a clearance is a sorting out, which here rearranges the letters

explanation.surface: Tidy up an untidy building site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clearance' rearranges MESSY and SITE; 'messy' looks like the anagram word but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To systemise is to arrange by a system, a close synonym of organise.

clue.text: One solution takes turn for article avoiding the rest

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: takes one thing for another signals a swap of letters
takes one thing for another signals a swap of letters

parts.note: a U-turn is a turn, so U stands for turn
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: One answer swaps a twist for a grammatical article, standing apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes turn for article' swaps the U of SOLUTION (U as in U-turn) for A.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolation is the condition of keeping apart from all others.

clue.text: Green side can be stimulated

indicators.note: can be suggests the letters may become something else

explanation.surface: An environmentally minded faction might be roused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be' rearranges GREEN SIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Energised and stimulated both mean filled with energy or roused to action.

clue.text: Boy leaves sleeper for sweeper

indicators.note: leaves means the boy's name is taken out

parts.note: a bedroom is where one sleeps
Ed is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A lad abandons a railway sleeper in favour of a sweeper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' takes ED out of BEDROOM. 'sleeper' suggests a railway sleeper or a sleeping person.
explanation.definitionFit: A brush on a long handle is used for sweeping floors.

clue.text: Being attractive keeps gunner's daughter matey

indicators.note: keeps means one word holds the others inside it

parts.note: comely means attractive
the RA, Royal Artillery, is the gunners' regiment

explanation.surface: A charming soldier's daughter is friendly.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Artillery are known as the gunners, a standard crossword source of RA.
explanation.definitionFit: Comradely means friendly as a companion, the same as matey.

clue.text: Plain clothes Muslim lawyer

definitions.meaning: civilian dress worn by someone usually in uniform
an expert in Islamic law who issues rulings

explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an expert in Islamic law and, by extension, civilian dress worn off duty.

clue.text: Long time and a quarter

parts.note: a year is a period of time
N, north, is one of the four quarters of the compass

explanation.surface: A long time and a fraction of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a quarter' is a compass point, here N; 'and' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: To long for something is to yearn for it.

clue.text: Second space must …

parts.note: a hall is a large room or space

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis leaves the sentence hanging, as if waiting for a verb after the modal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are modal verbs of obligation, as in 'you shall go' meaning you are required to go.

clue.text: Compiling lapse — a bit of a bloomer

indicators.note: compiling means putting the letters together in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A slip in compiling is a minor blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Compiling' rearranges LAPSE. 'bloomer' looks like a mistake but is a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: A sepal is one of the leafy parts at the base of a flower, so part of a bloom.

clue.text: Rude word to finish one's respectful address

parts.note: eff is a euphemism for a swear word
to end is to finish
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A swear word ends what should be a courteous greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Effendi is a Turkish title of respect, used as a polite form of address.

clue.text: Inform that paper is folded

indicators.note: folded paper is reshaped, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Tell someone the newspaper has gone out of business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'folded' rearranges PAPER IS; 'that' only joins. A paper that folds also closes down.
explanation.definitionFit: To apprise someone is to tell them or inform them of something.

clue.text: John Bull's paunch?

parts.note: John Bull personifies England, so his belly is the country's midriff; the phrase also names the conservative mainstream of English society

explanation.walkthrough: John Bull is the stout cartoon figure who stands for England.
explanation.definitionFit: The term means the conventional middle-class majority, and literally the waist of the national figure.
